heading: Food forest design
body: Build a living food system with layers.
Grow food from the crown of a tall tree down to root plants.
Use vertical space, soil life, shade and moisture together.
Learn to design and establish a food forest on your farm.

heading: Why this matters
body: A food forest grows useful plants at different heights.
A good design can combine harvests, shade and ground cover. Plants still compete for light, water and nutrients.
Plan the care you can give and watch how the planting changes.

heading: Learning outcomes
body: Name the seven layers that are often described for a food forest.
Check plants against your site, the local nature and the approved project list.
Plan establishment and ongoing care without imagining a particular day of harvest or of closing of the crown.

heading: The forest uses every layer
body: A native forest fills the space from the top branches to the roots.
Different plants use the light and moisture available at their layer.
A food forest imitates this way with productive plants.
The result is not one plant in one row, but many useful layers growing together.

heading: Watch: learn the seven planting layers
body: Find the seven planting layers.
Tall trees make the crown.
Small trees grow beneath it.
Then look for woody shrubs (stalks with wood).
Non-woody plants have soft stems.
Plants that cover the ground spread over the surface.
Root plants grow below the surface.
Climbing plants use suitable supports.
These are planning layers, they are not fixed height bands. Choose plants and their spacing according to your site.

heading: The seven layers
body: Think of a tall tree crown, small trees, shrubs and soft non-woody plants.
Ground-cover plants protect it above, root plants grow beneath it, and climbing plants use suitable supports.
Height and spacing of plants depend on the plants and the site. These are planning layers, they are not fixed height bands.

heading: Read an example of layered planting
body: The first Highveld example includes Wild Fig or pecan above lemon, naartjie and black mulberry.
It puts Cape gooseberry and Wild Medlar together with vegetables, wild garlic, sweet potato and granadilla.
Take this as a planning example, not permission to plant all kinds. Start by confirming which plant it is, frost resistance, size when grown, and local restrictions.

heading: Care changes as plants grow
body: Small plants need tending in their establishment: checking moisture, controlling weeds and protection from damage.
As plants grow, shade and fallen leaves change the conditions beneath them.
Check competition and access. Cut, thin or adjust the lower-layer planting when what you see requires; the system does not stop needing tending on a fixed day.

heading: Choose according to your site
body: Check rain, frost, heat, soil and water availability on your site before choosing plants.
Mango can be damaged by frost. Quince needs a suitably cold winter to fruit reliably.
The name of a region or a sheltered corner is not enough. Confirm each plant and each kind with a trusted local guide.

heading: Watch: match species and climate
body: Climate decides which species are suitable.
In the Highveld, choose trees and shrubs that tolerate cold; on the KZN coast and in the Lowveld, choose species of hot areas.
Match each plant to your site.

heading: Look at Highveld examples
body: The first list includes pecan, walnut and native fig; apple, pear, plum, black mulberry and loquat; rosemary, Wild Medlar, Cape gooseberry and Barbados cherry.
This list is not a recommendation for all. Check each plant for frost, soil, size when grown and the list of approved local species.
Keep the existing legal and project restrictions applying. Do not plant just from seeing a photo.

heading: Look at examples from hot areas
body: The first examples from hot areas include mango, avocado, Natal Mahogany, banana, pawpaw, litchi, Wild Fig, Barbados cherry and Wild Dagga.
Marula, Mopane and baobab also come from the Limpopo examples. Suitability for your site still needs checking.
Useful trees are not automatically edible. Confirm which plant it is and its safe use; a landscape photo is not a guide for identifying food.

heading: Include native plants suited to the site
body: Native plants suited to the site can support the living place of wild animals as part of the design.
Choose according to the nature of your site and the useful role of each plant. There is no percentage target based on a trusted source in this lesson.
Protect existing natural plants. Do not change healthy grassland into a food forest just because the trees are useful somewhere else.

heading: Plan the order on site
body: Start by checking the site, water supply and the care available. Protect bare soil immediately.
Temporary support plants can give shelter and useful cut material where suitable.
Main trees and the lower layers can be put in as conditions allow. Ground-cover plants need not wait until the end; avoid letting plants compete with small trees.

heading: Watch: look after a young food forest
body: This picture shows a young food forest. Start with a place you can look after.
Protect bare soil immediately. Here, loose mulch covers the soil.
Keep mulch away from the stem. Notice the clean area at the tree trunk.
Notice competition. The farmer removes grass beside the young tree.
Before adding more plants, check moisture, a safe place and the care you can give. Let what you see guide your next step.

heading: Prepare the first manageable area
body: Start with an area you can water and keep. Check existing plants before clearing.
Where suitable, ordinary cardboard under suitable mulch can reduce unwanted growth. Keep the water able to enter the soil and leave the tree stems clean.
Plan spacing by the size of the plants when grown. Prepare nursery plants for the next suitable planting gap.

heading: Adjust as trees grow
body: Look at how shade, roots and available water affect neighbouring plants.
Comfrey and wild garlic come from the first example of under-planting; check their suitability on your site before using them.

Cut or thin supporting plants when necessary, using methods suitable for each kind. Suitable clean cuttings can return as mulch. Do not wait for a particular fixed year if competition is already damaging plants.

heading: Plant with reliable moisture
body: Choose a planting time when soil moisture and expected weather support establishment.
Rain can help, but check the root area and always have a waiting watering plan. Avoid planting in waterlogged soil.
Check small plants after planting. Harvest timing and added inputs from outside depend on the kind of plant, the site and care; there is no guaranteed harvest in the fifth year.

heading: Fieldwork
body: Draw the layers of your proposed planting. Mark access, water and existing natural plants.
Record the frost, rain, soil and care available on your site.
For each plant on the approved list, record the intended role and the local advice that is still needed before planting.

heading: Field action
body: Check a manageable area and choose one next step.
Protect bare soil, check plant suitability, or prepare nursery plants.
Plant only when conditions and the following care are suitable. Return to that place and check survival, soil moisture and competition.
